items.prompt: Listen, then spell the word.
items.sentence: Use a sharp knife to cut the bread.
hints: Say the word slowly. The first sound you hear is n.
The first letter is silent, so you cannot hear it.
Start with the silent letter, then add the letters for the sound n.
items.explanation: Knife begins with a silent k. We write the k but we do not say it.

items.prompt: Which word has a silent letter?

options.why: Every letter in lunch is sounded when you say it.
You say every letter in lemon.
Every letter in lift is sounded.

hints: Say each word aloud and listen for every letter.
A silent letter is written but not heard.
Check the end of each word. One ends with a letter you do not say.
items.explanation: In lamb the b at the end is silent. We say lam but we write lamb.

items.prompt: Listen, then spell the word.
items.sentence: I gave the wrong answer and then I fixed it.
hints: It starts with a sound you hear as r.
There is a silent letter at the start.
Think of write and wrist. They begin the same way.
items.explanation: Wrong begins with a silent w. It is like write and wrist.

items.prompt:
Choose the right word for each gap.
___ going to carry ___ bags to the car and put them ___.
hints: Each word sounds the same but means something different.
They're is short for they are. Their shows owning. There shows a place.
Say they are in the first gap. Does it make sense?
items.explanation: They're means they are. Their shows that the bags belong to them. There tells us the place.

items.prompt: In the words want, war and water, how is the letter a said after the letter w?

options.why: Cat has a short a, but after w the sound changes.
There is no e sound in these words.
The sound is not like cup.

hints: Say want and then cat. Do the a sounds match?
After w, the letter a often changes its sound.
Listen for a sound that is close to the o in hot.
items.explanation: After w, the letter a often sounds like o. That is why want, war and water look odd but follow a pattern.

items.prompt: Listen, then spell the word.
items.sentence: The young bird could not fly yet.
hints: The first sound is y, as in yes.
The middle sounds like u in cup, but it is spelt with two letters.
The vowel pair is the same as in touch and country.
items.explanation: Young has the letters ou making a short u sound, like in touch and country.

items.prompt: Match each word to a word that rhymes with it.
hints: The letters ough can make different sounds.
Say the first word aloud, then each ending.
Start with through. It rhymes with a colour.
items.explanation: The letters ough have different sounds: tough says uff, through says oo, plough says ow and cough says off.

items.prompt: Sort the words by how ough is said.
hints: Say each word aloud before you sort it.
Tough rhymes with stuff. Cow rhymes with plough.
Cough and trough both end the way off does.
items.explanation: Ough can say uff in tough, rough and enough. It says off in cough and trough. It says ow in plough and bough.

items.prompt: Maya spells separate by thinking: there is a rat in sepArate. What does this trick help her remember?

options.text: that the word starts with s
options.why: The trick is about a letter in the middle of the word.

options.text: that the middle part is spelt with a
that the word ends with e
options.why: The trick does not help with the last letter.

options.text: that the word has two syllables
options.why: The trick is about a letter, not about syllables.

hints: A trick like this is called a mnemonic.
Look at the capital letter in sepArate.
The word rat hides the letters a, r and a.
items.explanation: The rat in sepArate reminds Maya to write a, not e, after sep. A memory trick helps with the tricky letter.

items.prompt: Look at these words: field, believe, piece, chief. What spelling rule do they follow?

options.text: i comes before e, as in field
e comes before i, as in veil
options.why: Veil is a different word. These four all have ie.

options.text: the word always ends with e
options.why: Only believe ends with e.

options.text: the word must have double letters
options.why: None of these words has a double letter.

hints: Look at the letters in the middle of each word.
Check which letter comes first, i or e.
Write the pairs out: f-ie-ld, bel-ie-ve.
items.explanation: All four words have ie, with i first. This pattern gives us a rule: i before e (when the sound is ee and the letter before is not c).

items.prompt: Look at these words: hope, hoping; make, making; bake, baking. What is the rule?

options.text: add ing and keep the e
options.why: Hoping and making do not keep the e.

options.text: drop the e, then add ing
double the last letter, then add ing
options.why: Hoping does not have a double p.

options.text: change e to y, then add ing
options.why: No word here has a y.

hints: Compare hope with hoping. What happened to the last letter?
Check make and making in the same way.
The final e goes away before ing.
items.explanation: When a word ends in e, we usually drop the e before adding ing: hope, hoping.

items.prompt: Put these words in alphabetical order.
hints: All four words begin with m, so look at the second letter.
Mango and market both start ma. Look at the third letter.
Compare n and r. Then compare milk and mirror in the same way.
items.explanation: Ma comes before mi. Mango has n and market has r, so mango comes first. Milk has l and mirror has r, so milk comes first.

items.prompt: The guide words on a dictionary page are draw and drum. Which word is on this page?

options.why: Dock starts do, which comes before dr.
Dusk starts du, which comes after dr.
Dry comes after drum because y comes after u.

hints: Guide words tell you the first and last word on the page.
Check the first two letters, then the third.
The word must come after draw and before drum.
items.explanation: Dream comes after draw (e after a) and before drum (e before u), so it is on this page.

items.prompt: Put the look, say, cover, write, check steps in the right order.
hints: Think about what you do before you hide the word.
You cannot check until you have written.
Start with looking.
items.explanation: First look at the word and say it. Then cover it, write it from memory and check.

items.prompt: Choose 3 words that are spelt correctly.

options.why: This is missing a silent letter. The word is thumb.
The word needs a silent letter at the start.
The word needs a silent letter at the start.

hints: Three of the words have a silent letter in the right place.
Check words that begin with k, w or g and then n or r.
Say each word. Does it still match a word you know?
items.explanation: Knock has a silent k, wrist has a silent w and gnat has a silent g. The other three words are missing silent letters.

items.prompt:
Two words are spelt wrongly. Type them correctly.
The yung lamb drank wotter from the stream.
Correct spellings: ___ and ___
hints: Look at the words that seem odd.
One word needs ou. The other has a after w.
Start with the first mistake in the sentence.
items.explanation: Young has ou for a short u sound. Water has a after w.

items.prompt: Say the word hospital. Which part is said most strongly?

options.why: The middle part is said softly.
The last part is said softly.
In longer words one part is said more strongly.

hints: Clap the beats of the word: hos-pi-tal.
One beat is louder and longer than the others.
Say it as if you are calling it out. Which part is loudest?
items.explanation: We stress the first part of hospital. The other two parts are unstressed and sound softer.

items.prompt: Sort the words by which part is stressed.
hints: Say each word and listen for the louder part.
In table, the first part is louder.
In about, the first part is short and soft.
items.explanation: In table, garden and carpet we say the first part more strongly. In about, begin and today we say the second part more strongly.

items.prompt: Tom keeps a list of words he spelt wrongly, with the correct spelling next to each. Why is this useful?

options.text: it shows him which words to learn
it means he never needs to practise
options.why: He still needs to practise the words.
The list does not change how long his writing is.

options.text: it lets him copy from friends
options.why: The list is for his own learning.

hints: A list like this is called a spelling log.
Think about what Tom does with the list later.
Which words keep appearing?
items.explanation: A spelling log shows the words you find hard, so you know what to learn next.

items.prompt: Dewi meets a new word: unbreakable. What is the best way to read it?

options.text: look at the first letter only
options.why: One letter is not enough to read the whole word.
Skipping may stop you understanding the sentence.

options.text: split it into parts: un, break, able
guess a word that looks like it
options.why: Guessing from the shape can give the wrong word.

hints: Look for a word you already know inside the longer word.
Find the prefix and the suffix.
Read each part, then blend them together.
items.explanation: Splitting unbreakable into un, break and able lets you read each small part and blend them.

items.prompt: Which sentence is spelt correctly?

options.why: Their shows owning. They're means they are.

options.text: There coats are on the hook.
options.why: There is a place. Their shows the coats belong to them.

options.text: They're coats are on the hook.
options.why: They're means they are. It does not show belonging.

options.text: They're sure their friends will wait there.

hints: Check each sentence by saying they are in place of they're.
Their shows that something belongs to them. There shows a place.
Try the last sentence first.
items.explanation: They're means they are. Their shows belonging. There is a place. The last sentence uses all three correctly.
